# [Episode 12: Ship It]{.flow} {.title}

## Launch week

One week to Demo Day. The first demos happen **today**, the rest in Session XIII, and the order comes out of a hat. The hat is Python.

. . .

Before anyone presents: twenty minutes on making your agent stop repeating the same mistakes.

# [Teach Your Agent]{.flow} {.title}

## The friction you know

- Two weeks in, you have corrected your agent on the same things again and again: naming style, the library you prefer, "keep functions short", "we filter with `.loc` here"
- Every session starts from zero: the agent remembers [nothing]{.highlight} between sessions (Session X, the loop)
- Explaining the same thing five times is work you should not be doing

## Package the rules once

- Put your project rules in **one markdown file** in the repo: `AGENTS.md`
- What goes in: what the project is, the stack, naming and style conventions, "any AI use lands in the README disclosure"
- Agents that support rules files read it at every session start, automatically
- If yours does not: same file, pasted into the first prompt of a session. Worst case, `AGENTS.md` is your clipboard file

## Skills: instructions on demand

- A **skill** is the next step up: a folder with a `SKILL.md`, holding a name, a description, and instructions
- Rules apply [always]{.highlight}. A skill loads only when the task matches its description, so context stays lean until the moment it is needed
- Example: a `verify` skill for your project: read the diff, run it, test it on a case where you know the answer, report what you checked

## Anatomy, briefly

```markdown
---
name: verify
description: Check changed code the way this project requires. Use after any code change.
---

- Read the diff line by line before running anything
- Run the code on a case where you know the correct answer
- Report what you checked and what the result was
```

. . .

Plain markdown you own, versioned with the project like any other file.

## Write your own

- Any workflow you have explained to the agent [twice]{.highlight} deserves a skill
- Keep it short: a page of instructions, not an essay
- Prune it when the workflow changes: a stale skill misleads
- Downloading one? Vet it by [reading it]{.highlight}, not by its star count

## What not to hand over

- The parts you must be able to **defend at the demo**: design choices, the statistics, why this approach
- A file can carry conventions. It cannot carry your judgment, and the demo questions come to you, not to it

# [Definition of Done]{.flow} {.title}

## Before you call it finished

- The repo runs from a fresh clone: `uv sync`, then the notebook or script, no hidden steps
- The README says what it does, how to run it, and carries the **AI disclosure section**
- The commit history tells the story: small steps, messages that mean something
- `git status` is clean: nothing uncommitted, nothing important ignored

. . .

:::{.callout-tip}
Run the fresh-clone test **today**, not on the morning of your demo. It always finds something.
:::

# [First Demos]{.flow} {.title}

## Today's batch

- Format: **10 minutes** presenting, **5 minutes** of questions, per pair
- Order: drawn at random with the `random` module from Session VI
- Show the thing running, the commit history, and one thing that broke
- Everyone else: watch for the recipe. You present in Session XIII

# [Wrap-up]{.flow} {.title}

## Three things to remember

- Rules in `AGENTS.md` for the [always]{.highlight} stuff, skills for the on-demand stuff, both plain markdown you own
- The fresh-clone test is the cheapest bug you will ever catch
- A demo is the thing running, the history, and the honest disclosure

. . .
